# Find Peak Element

> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/35f2ff41-64d2-4224-9988-855e1a3fbc61)** — free, no card: a runnable editor, the sample and hidden tests, a judged verdict, and the reference solution.

## Problem

Implement `findPeak(nums)`, which receives an integer array `nums` and returns the position (0-based index) of some peak element in it.

An element counts as a peak when it is strictly larger than each of the neighbors it actually has. In other words, index `i` is a peak if $$nums[i] > nums[i-1]$$ whenever index `i-1` is inside the array, and $$nums[i] > nums[i+1]$$ whenever index `i+1` is inside the array. Positions just outside the array are treated as negative infinity, so you may imagine $$nums[-1] = -\infty$$ and $$nums[n] = -\infty$$, where `n` is the length of `nums`.

The array may contain more than one peak; returning the index of any one of them is accepted. Your algorithm is required to run in $$O(\log n)$$ time.

### Input Format

The first line contains the integer `n`, the length of `nums`. The second line contains the `n` integers of `nums`, separated by spaces.

### Output Format

Print one integer: the index of any peak element.

Example 1:

```text
Input: nums = [1,2,3,1]

Output: 2
```

Explanation: `nums[2] = 3` is larger than both `nums[1] = 2` and `nums[3] = 1`, so index `2` is a peak.

Example 2:

```text
Input: nums = [1,2,1,3,5,6,4]

Output: 1
```

Explanation: `nums[1] = 2` exceeds both of its neighbors, so index `1` is a peak; index `5` (value `6`) would also be an acceptable answer.

Example 3:

```text
Input: nums = [1]

Output: 0
```

Explanation: A single element has only out-of-range neighbors, which count as negative infinity, so it is a peak.

Example 4:

```text
Input: nums = [2,1]

Output: 0
```

Explanation: `nums[0] = 2` is larger than `nums[1] = 1`, and its left side is out of range.

Example 5:

```text
Input: nums = [1,3,2]

Output: 1
```

Explanation: `nums[1] = 3` is larger than both `1` and `2`.

Example 6:

```text
Input: nums = [10,15,9,18,23,27,21]

Output: 1
```

Explanation: This array has two peaks, at index `1` (value `15`) and index `5` (value `27`). The output shown is only one valid answer; `5` is accepted as well.

Constraints:

* $$1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5$$, where `n` is the length of `nums`
* $$-10^9 \le nums[i] \le 10^9$$
* $$nums[i] \ne nums[i+1]$$ for every valid `i` (adjacent elements are never equal)
* The solution must run in $$O(\log n)$$ time; if several peaks exist, any one of their indices may be returned.

## Follow-ups

* Extend the solution to the 2D variant (LeetCode 1901): find a peak element in a 2D matrix.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Think of the array as a landscape where you can use binary search to find a peak without checking every element.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Compare the middle element with its neighbor to decide which half must contain a peak.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

The algorithm runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space, and works because the array boundaries are treated as -∞.

</details>
